findings.title: assemble's fixed batch_size=10000 hard-fails every definition with MaxRows above 10000
findings.why_it_matters: The row cap that guards the in-memory multi-source assembly is hard-coded at 10000 in `assemble`'s signature, and neither caller overrides it (`builder_service.py:233` and `report_service.py:111` both call it positionally). Meanwhile three separate schemas advertise a 100,000 ceiling: `ReportDefinitionUpsert.max_rows` (`schemas/report_builder.py:165`, `le=100_000`), `MAX_ROWS_CEILING = 100_000` in `definition_service.py:53`, and the execute request's temporary override (`report_builder.py:239`, `le=100_000`). At the expected scale that means a definition saved with MaxRows=50000 passes write-time validation and 202-accepts at execute time, then the worker dies with `REPORT_JOIN_TOO_LARGE` after doing the full 50k-row fetch and Python assembly — the user waits the full render window and gets a 400 for a configuration the system explicitly said was legal. The failure is worst exactly where the design intends it to scale, and it is also a silent-memory hazard in the other direction: the real memory ceiling is never enforced against the value users actually set. Passing `batch_size=limit` (or deriving it from the definition's MaxRows with a hard absolute ceiling) makes the cap track the declared contract, and the memory guarantee is preserved because `limit` is what already bounds the primary-source fetch.
findings.suggested_fix: Thread the effective row limit into `assemble` from the one place that already knows it. In `builder_service.execute_definition`, the call at line 233 is `qe.assemble(rows_by_source, join_keys, primary, fields_by_source)`; change it to `qe.assemble(rows_by_source, join_keys, primary, fields_by_source, batch_size=limit)`, since `limit` (line 193) is `temporary_max_rows or row.max_rows or 10000` and `main_rows` has already been truncated to it at line 222 — so the check becomes unreachable-but-consistent instead of a contradiction with the 100k ceiling. Note the asymmetry this creates and decide it deliberately: `report_service._MAX_ROWS` stays 10000, so the fixed-10 path remains capped there, while the builder path honours the per-definition MaxRows. If the intent was actually to hard-cap ALL report generation at 10k for memory reasons, the cheaper and more honest fix is the opposite one: lower `le=100_000` to `le=10000` in both `schemas/report_builder.py:165` and `report_builder.py:239` and drop `MAX_ROWS_CEILING` to 10000, so the schema stops advertising a range that provably cannot execute. Verify with a test that executes a definition at `max_rows=10001` and asserts either success-with-10001-rows or a 400 at write time — not at render time.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/services/report/query_engine.py:313 — `    if len(base_rows) > batch_size:` with `batch_size: int = 10000` declared at query_engine.py:297 and raised as `REPORT_JOIN_TOO_LARGE` (400) at :317.
pcs-backend/app/services/report/builder_service.py:233 — `    merged = qe.assemble(rows_by_source, join_keys, primary, fields_by_source)` — no `batch_size` argument, so the 10000 default applies.

pcs-backend/app/services/report/builder_service.py:193 — `    limit = temporary_max_rows or row.max_rows or 10000` and :222 `    main_rows = main_rows[:limit]` — `base_rows` reaching `assemble` has exactly `limit` rows, so `limit > 10000` deterministically trips the guard.

pcs-backend/app/schemas/report_builder.py:165 — `    max_rows: int = Field(default=10000, ge=1, le=100_000)` and pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report_builder.py:239 — `    max_rows: int | None = Field(default=None, ge=1, le=100_000)` both admit values the executor can never serve.
grep for `batch_size` across app/services/report and app/api/v1 returns only query_engine.py:297 (the default) and :313 (the check) — no caller anywhere raises or lowers it.

findings.title: report_service chunked IN loop reuses the mutated statement, ANDing every chunk together
findings.why_it_matters: The batching loop reassigns `stmt` to its own `.where()` result, so each iteration builds on the previous statement's predicates instead of starting from the clean `build_select` base. At the constants as written the loop only ever runs once (`_MAX_ROWS = 10000` bounds `keys` and `_BATCH_SIZE = 10000` is the stride, so `range(0, 10000, 10000)` yields `[0]`), which makes the defect invisible today — the chunking is dead code, and any test that appears to cover it passes without executing a second iteration. The moment the two constants diverge, which the documented 100k MaxRows ceiling invites, chunk N+1's statement carries chunk 1's `IN` predicate as an additional `AND`, so every chunk after the first returns zero rows and the statement grows to N×5000 bind parameters — silently defeating the exact reason the batching exists (the module comment says so on line 170). This is a copy-paste divergence from the correct sibling implementation at `builder_service._fetch_join_rows`, which builds the predicate into a local and passes it as `stmt.where(where)` without rebinding; the same logic exists twice in the same package with opposite correctness. Fixing it now, before any constant is tuned, is a two-line change that keeps the multi-chunk path honest.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not rebind `stmt` inside the loop — pass the per-chunk predicate to `execute` directly, mirroring the working sibling at `builder_service.py:135`. Change line 173 from `stmt = stmt.where(_join_column(source, join_field).in_(chunk))` to `where = _join_column(source, join_field).in_(chunk)`, and line 174 from `result = await db.execute(stmt)` to `result = await db.execute(stmt.where(where))`. Verify by adding a unit test that calls `_fetch_join_rows` with more keys than `_BATCH_SIZE` (monkeypatch `_BATCH_SIZE` down to a small value rather than seeding tens of thousands of rows) and asserts the union of returned rows covers every key across all chunks; that test fails against the current code and passes after the change. As a follow-up, consider deleting `_BATCH_SIZE` from `report_service.py` or making both modules share one helper — as written the duplication is exactly what let the two implementations drift.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:173 — `        stmt = stmt.where(_join_column(source, join_field).in_(chunk))` rebinds the loop-invariant statement; line 174 then executes the accumulated statement.

pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:171 — `    for i in range(0, len(keys), _BATCH_SIZE):` with `_BATCH_SIZE = 10000` at :69 and `paginate(stmt, limit=_MAX_ROWS)` where `_MAX_ROWS = 10000` at :96 — so `len(keys) <= 10000` and the loop body runs exactly once today.

pcs-backend/app/services/report/builder_service.py:135 — `        result = await db.execute(stmt.where(where))` — the correct sibling form, with `where` built as a local at :132-134 and `stmt` left untouched since :127.

Measured chunk counts for the current constants: `range(0, 10000, 10000)` yields 1 chunk; raising the row cap to 100000 yields 10 chunks, each executed against a statement carrying all prior chunks' `IN` predicates.

residual_risks: Both read endpoints added by this phase return unbounded result sets with no limit/offset: `GET /report-builder/definitions` (`definition_service.py:206-214`, plain `.scalars()` with no cap) and `GET /report/styles` (`report.py:323`, plain `.scalars().all()` with the permission filter then applied in Python at :324-325). Both tables are configuration-shaped and grow slowly, so this is unlikely to bite soon — but `report_styles` accumulates a row per revision via `POST /styles/{style_id}/revise`, and neither endpoint has a pagination contract in the response schema beyond a `total` computed from the full in-memory list, so there is no place to add one later without a breaking API change. Worth deciding the pagination contract now while the schemas are still new.

The two hourly reclaimers `reclaim_stale_tasks` and `reclaim_stale_execution_logs` (`report_tasks.py:227-232` and :282-288) each load every stale row with an unbounded `.scalars().all()` and then write one audit row per stale row inside the loop. Both are bounded in practice by how many tasks went stale, which is only large if the ARQ worker is down for an extended period — precisely the scenario the reclaimers exist for. Not verified against real volume; flagged as a shape to watch rather than a defect.

`collect`, `assemble`, `_to_blocks` and `_content_hash` all run inline on the event loop rather than being dispatched to a thread the way `_render_sync` is. I measured this specifically because the 10-CPU-second PDF rationale makes it a plausible finding: `dataclasses.asdict` plus `json.dumps` over a synthetic 10,000-row × 6-column TableBlock costs ~10 ms combined, so at the default 10k MaxRows it is immaterial and I am not raising it as a finding. It would become material only if the 100k ceiling from finding 1 is ever actually honoured, in which case the inline canonicalization scales roughly 10× to ~100 ms — still small next to a render — but the same review should re-check `_fetch_join_rows`' `list(DATASOURCES[source].fields)` column projection at that row count, which I did not measure.
testing_gaps: The performance benchmark does not exercise the multi-source path at all. `test_xlsx_10k_rows_under_10s` seeds `EQUIPMENT_LIST`, whose spec (`collector.py:84-88`) declares a single source `EQUIP_LIST` with no `extra_sources` — so at 10,000 rows the suite never runs the batched `IN (...)` join fetch, never runs `query_engine.assemble`'s dict-index merge, and never runs the per-source column projection. Those are exactly the code paths the `query_engine` module docstring claims cost '约 1–2s' at 10k rows, and that claim is currently backed by no assertion. A benchmark variant seeding EQUIP_LIST plus one whitelisted join source (e.g. `HEAT_RESULTS`) at 10k rows would pin the assemble path to the SPEC §3.3.1 budget.

No test binds the advertised `max_rows` ceiling to the executor. `le=100_000` appears in two schemas and `MAX_ROWS_CEILING = 100_000` in `definition_service.py`, but every test that sets `max_rows` uses 250, 50 or 100 (`tests/api/v1/test_report_builder.py:446`, `:718`; `tests/workers/test_report_tasks.py:484`). `REPORT_JOIN_TOO_LARGE` is only asserted by calling `assemble` directly (`tests/services/report/test_query_engine.py:196`), which bypasses the schema entirely — so the round-trip from an accepted `max_rows` to an executed one is uncovered above 100.

The multi-chunk IN path in `report_service._fetch_join_rows` has no test that forces a second iteration; by construction (`_MAX_ROWS == _BATCH_SIZE == 10000`) no existing test can reach one, which is why finding 2 stays latent. A test that monkeypatches `_BATCH_SIZE` to a small value and asserts the union across chunks would pin the intended semantics.

No test asserts the `_REGISTERED` font cache is not re-populated on the failure path. `test_font_registration_is_cached_across_renders` covers the success path only; `_unregister_font` at `renderer_pdf.py:138` is exercised by no benchmark, so a regression that re-parses the 10.6MB TTF on every render (the ~0.3s first-render cost the test docstring cites) would only show up as a slow `test_simple_report_under_5s`.
